record.original_question: Let Rf(alpha,p) be the classical Radon transform of a function f on R^2, defined by integrating f with respect to arclength over the line ell_{alpha,p} = {x in R^2 : alpha dot x = p}, where alpha is a unit vector and p is real. Suppose f is continuous on R^2, f restricted to every line ell_{alpha,p} is in L^1(ell_{alpha,p}), and there are constants c > 0 and m >= 0 such that |f(x)| <= c(1 + |x|^m) for all x. If Rf(alpha,p) = 0 for every unit vector alpha and every real p, must f be identically zero? Equivalently, what is the weakest natural growth restriction at infinity under which these line-integrability and vanishing-Radon-transform assumptions force f = 0?

evidence.quote: where `α,p is a straight line α · x = p on the plane x = {x1, x2}, α is a unit vector, p is a real number, ds is the element of the arclength of the straight line.
Assume that f ∈ L 1 (`α,p) (2) for all p and α, that f is a continuous function, and that |f(x)| ≤ c(1 + |x| m), (3)

The open problem is to understand what the weakest natural restriction on the growth of f at infinity is for the Radon transform to be injective.

artifact.status_search_result: The injectivity question for the planar Radon transform under merely polynomial growth (with line-integrability) is posed as an open problem by Ramm and remains unresolved; available results address compactly supported or rapidly decaying functions, while the weakest natural growth condition forcing f = 0 is not known.
